children: CEO Jim Farley believes the U.S. still has time to defend its auto industry against fast-expanding Chinese rivals, even as Europe struggles to contain their growing market presence. His warning highlights a complicated challenge for Detroit automakers: competing against China's lower-cost electric vehicles while selectively tapping Chinese technology to improve their own competitiveness.

Ford, one of America's largest automakers, generates revenue primarily through vehicle sales, commercial fleet operations and financing. Its portfolio spans gasoline-powered vehicles, hybrids and EVs, with the company increasingly emphasizing affordable electrification alongside its profitable truck business.
Speaking at the Automotive News Congress in Detroit on Tuesday, Farley urged U.S. policymakers to consider Europe's experience before deciding how widely to open the American market.

I think it's just important for us to take our time to be considerate, Farley said, according to CNBC. I watch what's happening in Europe right now, where that was not the case, and it's really something that they have to deal with now, and it's too late.

The figures illustrate his concern. Chinese automakers' global market share increased nearly 70% between 2020 and 2025, according to GlobalData, while their European market share reached 12% in August, Dataforce reported.
Farley's strategy, however, is not to abandon Chinese partnerships entirely.
Ford and Geely announced plans in July to manufacture EVs at Ford's Spanish facility through a joint venture, with production targeted for early 2027.

Our answer is pretty simple. We're going to partner with the Chinese where we don't have [intellectual property], where we can be more capital efficient in places like Europe or Southeast Asia, Farley explained.
Ford's answer at home is its Universal EV platform, beginning with the Fathom midsize electric pickup, advertised at a starting price of $28,350, with preorders planned for early 2027.
Investors should monitor whether Ford can achieve competitive production costs and sustainable margins at that price point.

Its Chinese partnerships also carry regulatory uncertainty. U.S. lawmakers are considering additional restrictions on Chinese automotive companies, potentially complicating cross-border investments and supply arrangements.
The central test is whether Ford can absorb Chinese manufacturing advantages abroad while building a sufficiently competitive, lower-cost EV business at home.

title: Ford CEO Sends Stark Warning to U.S. Auto Industry
